chunks: Vout from duty cycle and Vin. The question: Given duty cycle and Vin, can you find Vout?
For a buck in continuous conduction, the output voltage is the duty cycle times the input voltage.
This is the same rule as finding D from the voltage ratio ("Duty cycle from a Vout/Vin ratio"), used the other way round.
It is only the starting point, though, because real drops and light load both change the answer.
Imagine a room that is heated for part of every minute. If it is heated one quarter of the time, its average temperature rise is one quarter of what full heating would give.
The buck averages a pulse train the same way.
The analogy breaks at light load: there the inductor current stops for part of each cycle, and the simple average no longer gives the output.
The grey line is the textbook D V in .
Light loads (small K ) sit above it, especially at small D : the output is far larger than the duty cycle predicts and the transfer curve is nonlinear. Heavier loads hug the line.
At D equals 27. 5 % the 33 ohms load reaches 6. 12 volts; the 150 ohms load is higher still.
Drag L or f up: K grows, the curves close in on the grey line (the 8 ohms load stays in CCM at every duty cycle), and the gain depends far less on the load.
Drag them down and the light-load curves bow far above it.
Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the switch is on ("What is duty cycle"). Input voltage ( V in ): the voltage feeding the converter.
Average value: the long-run level of a pulse train, D times V in . Continuous conduction: the inductor current stays above zero ("What sets a buck's output voltage").
Discontinuous mode: the current falls to zero for part of each cycle.
With V in equals 12 volts and D equals 0. 25 , the output is 0. 25 times 12 equals 3 volts. With D equals 0. 5 it is 6 volts. For 27. 5 percent, it is 3. 3 volts.
In a real synchronous buck the switch and inductor resistances shave off a few tens of millivolts; a diode buck loses several hundred. That is the whole idea.
"Yes, in continuous conduction: V out equals D V in , so 27. 5 percent of 12 volts is 3. 3 volts. Real drops pull it down a bit.
In discontinuous mode at light load the output is higher for the same duty cycle, so I'd need the load, inductance and frequency too.
And in a closed-loop regulator, D isn't an independent input; the feedback loop sets it to hold V out ."
Quick check. An open-loop diode buck at fixed D has its load removed entirely. What happens to V out ?
